population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. Survey data from late 2028 put about 21% of US adults currently on an incretin for any reason. About 32% have ever used one. So roughly 1 adult in 9 is a former user who is currently off. Persistence has improved but cycling is still the norm. One-year persistence among weight-management starters rose from ~35% to ~46%, mostly because cost-driven stopping fell once unbranded semaglutide hit $59. About 44% of ever-users have stopped at least once and restarted. The income gradient has narrowed but not closed. Medicaid coverage and $0 provision at community health centres pulled the bottom third up from an estimated ~6% to ~18%. The lowest-use group is now the band between subsidy eligibility and good coverage: working adults at 200–350% of the poverty line in plans that dropped coverage. They show the highest stop-start rates. Medicaid work requirements, in force from 2027, add churn: an estimated 1 in 7 Medicaid users had a coverage gap of 60+ days in 2028. The top third includes a growing group without obesity. Roughly 3–4% of all adults, mostly affluent, take low 'metabolic health', longevity or 'calm' doses, often outside insurance and partly through the gray market. 65+ use roughly doubled under the extended Medicare bridge. Under-18 use is ~1.2% overall, mostly adolescents 12–17 with obesity, still skewed to the insured. About 4 in 10 US children now live in a household with at least one current user. US adult obesity prevalence is estimated at ~33%, down from 36.4%.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the GLP-1 Bridge demonstration was extended through Dec 2028 rather than allowed to lapse. In Dec 2027 Congress lifted the statutory Part D exclusion of weight-loss drugs, effective Jan 2029. It passed after CBO cut its score by more than half once unbranded semaglutide repriced the market. Medicare pays ~$245 for branded tirzepatide/semaglutide under the 2025 deals and the 2027 negotiated price. The preferred tier is unbranded semaglutide at ~$70, with a $0–10 copay. Medicaid: ~38 state programs cover unbranded semaglutide for obesity, most at $0 copay. Several others cover it only under the alcohol-use-disorder pathway. A federal HRSA grant line (the 'Metabolic Health Access' program) provides unbranded semaglutide free at community health centres to uninsured adults under 200% FPL, conditional on a nutrition-visit enrollment. Public programs now pay for a majority of new starts.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Generic semaglutide is sold in ~160 countries. India: ~$5–30/month, 60+ brands. China: multiple domestic generics since its 2026 patent lapse, and a major peptide-API exporter. Canada: CAD 60–90/month. Brazil and Mexico: generic and local brands. EU, UK and Japan remain brand-only until ~2031. Personal-import mail-order from India and Canada reaches US consumers at $15–40/month.
access.note: US price collapse runs through near-generics, not legal generics. Semaglutide and tirzepatide exclusivity still runs to ~2031–32. In Aug 2027, Novo Nordisk launched an unbranded semaglutide (injectable pens, cash $59/month) under its own label. The playbook matches insulin's authorised generics, aimed at undercutting imports and holding volume. Lilly cut Foundayo starter doses to $79 and higher doses to $99–129. Generic liraglutide (daily, ~5–8% loss) sells at $39–60. Premium tiers remain: retatrutide (approved 2028) lists at ~$1,499 with ~$499 cash via the manufacturer, and MariTide (monthly, approved Oct 2028) lists at ~$1,249. Employers cite the $59 sticker as the reason for dropping coverage; many now offer an HSA stipend instead. Gray market: FDA tolerates personal importation under 90-day enforcement discretion. At the same time CBP seizures of counterfeit pens rose roughly 9× between 2026 and 2028. Non-prescription 'wellness' demand from people ineligible for coverage is the gray market's core customer base. Weekly injectables are ~58% of volume, daily orals ~40%, monthly <2% at year end.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic; Novo unbranded semaglutide from Aug 2027)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1/amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Dec 2026; modest uptake after failing non-inferiority vs tirzepatide)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Apr 2028)
GLP-1 agonist / GIPR antagonist antibody-peptide conjugate, monthly injectable (maridebart cafraglutide: MariTide, approved Oct 2028)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda and generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: adolescent obesity 12+ (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide label expansion 2027)

alcohol use disorder — guideline-endorsed, not yet FDA-approved: ASAM and VA/DoD (Nov 2027) list semaglutide as a second-line pharmacotherapy for AUD, first-line where obesity co-occurs; pivotal-trial readout and sNDA expected 2029
mainstream_offlabel_uses: low-dose 'metabolic health' and longevity use by people without obesity: telehealth subscriptions, concierge medicine and gray-market pens; est. 3–4% of US adults
'calm / focus / freedom from craving' plans: low-dose semaglutide or Foundayo marketed by telehealth wellness brands for food noise, phone and shopping compulsions, and work focus
alcohol reduction in people without diagnosed AUD ('dry-curious' prescribing)
nicotine and vaping cessation: observational support, trials ongoing
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care, still rare
drugs.pipeline_note: Retatrutide's label carries dysesthesia and higher GI discontinuation. Uptake is concentrated in cash-pay and premium commercial plans. MariTide's monthly dosing is pitched to payers as an adherence fix, but it is barely in pharmacies at year end. Amycretin (injectable and oral) is in phase 3 with readouts 2029. Survodutide filed for MASH and obesity. Bimagrumab plus semaglutide (muscle preservation) is in phase 3 and marketed as the upcoming answer to lean-mass loss. No implant has reached filing. Analyst 2030 global incretin revenue forecasts fell from $150–162B to ~$115–130B even as volume forecasts rose: price per patient fell faster than patients grew. Novo announced a second restructuring (Mar 2028). Lilly's revenue keeps growing on tirzepatide, orforglipron and retatrutide.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and leading cause of discontinuation. Higher with retatrutide. Dosing errors with imported and counterfeit product add GI hospitalisations.
Elevated with rapid weight loss. Cholecystectomy volume up measurably in Medicare claims since the bridge pilot.
No causal confirmation in long-term RCTs. Absolute risk low. Case reports cluster with counterfeit and overdosed product.

Medicare observational data from the bridge cohort show a small rise in fall-related fractures among users over 75 who lost >15% of body weight. Effect sizes are disputed and confounded. Concern is concentrated in older adults and repeated cyclers, who regain mostly fat.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. Several Medicare contractors recommend resistance-training and protein counselling at initiation. Muscle-sparing adjuncts are in phase 3.

safety_ledger.effect: NAION (non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy) / sudden optic-nerve vision loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A pooled FDA Sentinel and multinational cohort analysis (2026–27) found a consistent ~1.7–2× relative risk across GLP-1 receptor agonists. Baseline incidence is low (~2–10 per 100,000 per year), so excess risk is on the order of a few extra cases per 100,000 users per year. At US scale that means thousands of additional cases annually. Risk is higher in people with diabetes, a 'crowded' optic disc, or prior NAION in one eye.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class-wide Warnings and Precautions label (Feb 2027) for all GLP-1 receptor agonist products, with patient Medication Guide language on sudden vision loss. Ophthalmology societies advise baseline eye exams for high-risk patients. Products liability filings rose sharply.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association in EMA, MHRA and FDA reviews. Larger datasets since 2026 have not reopened it.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning removed (2026). Gray-market product carries no labelling at all.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: First quantified in 2027–28. A large patient-reported cohort using validated anhedonia scales found clinically meaningful score increases in ~9% of users vs ~5% of matched non-users, dose-related and mostly reversible on dose reduction. A secondary analysis of an AUD trial found reduced reward response to non-drug cues as well as alcohol. The effect is now both a reported harm and a marketed benefit.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. FDA requested anhedonia measures in postmarketing studies for new approvals. FTC warning letters (2028) to three telehealth brands over unsubstantiated 'focus' and 'calm' claims.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Real-world data converge between trial and claims estimates. Roughly half to two-thirds of lost weight returns within 12–18 months of stopping. Coverage-gap cyclers show repeated regain.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. Drives chronic-therapy framing. Medicaid continuity-of-care rules are debated.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Case series of thiamine, B12 and iron deficiency in users eating very little, especially older adults and people on low-dose wellness plans with restrictive diets.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: HRSA program requires a nutrition visit. No label change.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; adolescent use over decades; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of RCT follow-up now exists. No signal beyond known effects, and no data on cycling or adolescent-to-adult use.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on new approvals. NIH funded a 10-year pediatric registry (2027).

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded, imported and counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination, wrong active ingredient)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Over 5,000 FDA adverse-event reports by 2028. A 2027 CDC health alert linked 312 emergency visits in 14 states to counterfeit pens, some containing insulin (severe hypoglycaemia), with two deaths. Endotoxin-contaminated vials and 2–10× concentration errors are recurrent.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion finalised (2027). CBP and FDA import operations, with seizures up ~9× since 2026. Personal importation is still tolerated, a policy contradiction FDA has not resolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Seen in phase 3, mostly mild and transient, more common at higher doses.

safety_ledger.effect: Low-dose use in people without obesity (longevity / 'calm' plans)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No RCTs in lean or normal-weight populations. Benefit claims rest on extrapolation, while lean-mass and micronutrient risks may be proportionally larger.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None specific. Off-label prescribing is legal. FTC acts on advertising, not use.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~36% of US households. Cumulative packaged-snack and confectionery volume is down ~7% since 2024, and sugary carbonated drinks down ~5%. Revenue losses are partly offset by price per unit, protein reformulation and mini formats. Two large snack makers divested legacy brands. Plant consolidations cut several thousand manufacturing jobs, concentrated in the Midwest and South. Private label gains as smaller baskets trade down. 'Protein per calorie' is the dominant claim on shelf.

alcohol.state: US spirits volume down ~4% a year in 2027–28 and beer down faster. Heavy-drinker trading-down, now reinforced by the AUD guideline and a plausible on-label approval in 2029, hits the top-decile drinkers who carry the category. Distillers pivot to premium small formats, low-ABV and ready-to-drink. Craft brewery closures accelerate, and distributors consolidate.

restaurants.state: Traffic roughly flat overall, but all-you-can-eat and value-heavy casual dining lose traffic. Half-portion and 'small plate at full price' menus are standard. Average check holds via premium proteins and one 'occasion' cocktail. Drink attachment rates are falling. Delivery order sizes are shrinking.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep contracting, with store closures and one chain restructuring. The mainstream re-buy wave at smaller sizes has largely passed. Alterations and tailoring see a small boom. Fitted, muscle-showing cuts and performance wear lead growth in upper-income segments.

fitness.state: Strength training, coached small-group and 'lean-mass' programmes grow fastest, with DEXA body-composition scans as an upscale add-on. Budget gyms are flat. Premium strength studios and in-home coaching are the growth, priced well above what the $59 user can spend.

insurance.state: Commercial plans and employers retreat to 44% coverage and point members to cash at $59. Some offer HSA stipends. Pharmacy trend moderates as unit cost falls. Medicare and Medicaid absorb volume. Part D plans prepare premium increases for the 2029 exclusion lift. Prior-auth fights shift to the premium agents (retatrutide, MariTide).

pharma.state: Volume is up sharply and price per patient sharply down. Novo is in a second restructuring after cannibalising its own brand with unbranded semaglutide. Lilly leads on tirzepatide, oral orforglipron and retatrutide. Amgen enters with monthly dosing. Indian and Chinese generic makers win the rest of the world and supply the US gray market indirectly. 2030 revenue forecasts revised down.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Thinness no longer signals money because it costs $59 or is free at the health centre. What it signals now is which drug, how much muscle, and how the weight came off. A lean body with visible shoulders and arms, even skin, and steady weight reads as premium agents, coaching, protein and time. A thin-soft body, a face that lost volume fast, or a body visibly between regain and loss reads as generic, cycling or gray market. A large body increasingly reads as uninsured, rural or deliberate.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Body shape has become an income proxy, but the gradient moved: access is almost universal, while quality, continuity and muscle are not. Generic-semaglutide users in the coverage gap cycle with their finances. Affluent users stay continuous on retatrutide, add strength coaching and enter trials for muscle-sparing adjuncts. Lean affluent people take low 'longevity' doses they don't medically need. A visible minority rejects the drugs as identity: body-neutral activists, some religious communities, some athletes. 'Never-on' is a claim of authenticity in some circles and an admission of poverty in others.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals are smaller and shorter. Holiday tables plan for half the food. Families have mixed appetites at one table, with children often the only ones finishing plates. Snacking as social glue has thinned at offices and schools. Restaurants sell 'the occasion' rather than the volume. In households where adults are on-drug, children's food environments are shrinking too: fewer snacks bought, fewer family dinners cooked at scale. Pediatricians are watching for under-eating and over-eating.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles commonly state 'on', 'off' or 'never', and some apps added filters in 2028. Alcohol-free first dates are normal among under-40s. Couples therapists describe 'appetite mismatch': one partner on-drug and calm, the other not, with a shared life built around food and drink coming apart. Reduced libido is reported often enough to be a dinner-party topic. Low-dose 'calm' users are sometimes described by partners as easier and more distant at once.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite of any kind is now widely treated as an adjustable setting rather than a trait. Craving for food, drink, scrolling or shopping is something one can dial down for $59 a month. Wanting a lot is quietly coded as either unmedicated or chosen.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: First quantified in 2027–28. Roughly 9% of users report clinically meaningful anhedonia increases vs ~5% of matched non-users. The effect is dose-related and mostly reversible. Separately, a large and unmeasured share of low-dose users take the drug for this effect: telehealth brands sell 'quiet' and 'calm' subscriptions to people without obesity, for food noise, alcohol, phone use and focus. The clinic calls it a side effect, the AUD guideline calls it a mechanism, and the wellness market calls it the product.
interior_life.framing: Feature, in the market. Telehealth and wellness brands sell craving-free calm and focus. Manufacturers stay silent because off-label promotion is illegal for them. In clinics it is still a side effect to dose-adjust, and in addiction medicine it is a treatment. FTC warning letters target specific claims without disturbing the category.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Low-dose 'focus' plans are popular among knowledge workers, traders and some sales staff, bought privately. No employer formally encourages them, but a few tech and finance firms' wellness stipends can be spent on them. Managers report fewer after-work drinks and flatter client dinners, and sales and hospitality veterans complain the 'entertaining' economy is quieter. An early working paper linking claims to payroll data finds no detectable earnings or productivity effect in either direction. Anecdotes of lost ambition and of newfound steadiness remain about equally common.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Nightlife has shifted toward earlier, shorter, lower-alcohol evenings. Intensity products are selling: extreme sour, heat, loud live shows, cold plunges, ultra-endurance events. Some explain this as users chasing a signal that registers. Being off-drug has become a minor credential among musicians, comedians and chefs, and 'unmedicated appetite' is a marketing line for some restaurants. Stand-up and TV satire about 'quiet' partners and silent dinner parties is a recognisable genre. Sports-betting and mobile-game firms note small engagement declines among on-drug cohorts in their own data and do not discuss them publicly.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Reduced desire is commonly reported. Partners of low-dose 'calm' users describe them as easier to live with and harder to reach. Some couples synchronise, both on or both off. Mixed couples report friction around food, drink and spontaneity. Clinicians increasingly advise dose reduction rather than stopping when libido complaints arise.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable effect on turnout or partisanship has been shown. The idea that it might exist is itself a political force: populist voices on both the right and the left call the free HRSA provision and Medicaid coverage 'sedating the poor'. Some MAHA-aligned figures attack the program their own administration expanded. Alcohol, snack and sugar-state lobbies quietly fund some of that messaging. Campaigns test 'calm voter' targeting theories that nobody can verify.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access and fast on approvals: retatrutide in a standard cycle, MariTide under a priority voucher. Safety labelling is firmer: a class NAION warning in 2027. Enforcement on supply is contradictory: aggressive against compounders and counterfeiters, tolerant of personal importation of foreign generics, and largely hands-off on off-label low-dose prescribing apart from FTC advertising actions.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Direct subsidy and free provision with no mandate. Free unbranded semaglutide at community health centres for uninsured adults under 200% FPL (HRSA grant line, launched Jan 2028). $0–10 copays in most Medicaid programs and the extended Medicare bridge. Part D exclusion lifted effective 2029. Federal incretin spending is estimated at ~$14B in 2028, far below 2025 projections per patient because unit prices collapsed.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: The HRSA program requires a nutrition-visit enrollment and a 6-month weight and refill check to continue. Medicaid coverage is subject to 2027 work-requirement reporting, so missed reports interrupt therapy and produce state-induced cycling. Pharmacy refill data drive continuation decisions in Medicare. No biometric monitoring of off-label or cash users.
state.workforce_or_military: DoD accession guidance (2027) allows waivers for applicants who met body-composition standards on a GLP-1 and remain stable on it, and recruiters cite the policy in markets with high obesity. No mandates on service members or civilian workers.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: India and China dominate generic supply worldwide and indirectly feed the US gray market. China is also the main source of peptide API in counterfeits. US exclusivity to ~2031–32 now protects brands mainly in the US premium tier. Novo's and Lilly's US manufacturing investments are traded for tariff relief. The visible US–abroad price gap has narrowed from ~40× to ~2–4× for semaglutide.

events.event: FDA adds a class-wide Warnings and Precautions label for sudden optic-nerve vision loss (NAION) to all GLP-1 receptor agonists, citing a pooled Sentinel and international cohort analysis showing roughly doubled relative risk.

CDC health alert links 312 emergency visits in 14 states, and two deaths, to counterfeit and mislabeled imported semaglutide pens, some found to contain insulin; CBP announces a surge in mail-facility seizures.
Novo Nordisk launches unbranded semaglutide pens at $59 a month cash, undercutting personal imports; Lilly cuts Foundayo starter doses to $79 within three weeks.
ASAM and VA/DoD guidelines endorse semaglutide for alcohol use disorder; within weeks, major telehealth platforms roll out low-dose 'calm' and 'focus' subscriptions for people without obesity.

Congress lifts the Part D exclusion on weight-loss drugs effective 2029 and extends the Medicare GLP-1 bridge through 2028; HHS announces free unbranded semaglutide at community health centres for uninsured adults under 200% of poverty from January.
FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, the first once-monthly obesity injection, at a $1,249 list price; payers call it an adherence fix and place it on the highest tier.

open_tensions: Access is nearly universal on paper but continuous only for the well-off. The coverage gap between subsidy eligibility and good insurance, plus Medicaid work-requirement churn, keeps millions cycling. Nobody knows what years of cycling do, and the 2029 Part D expansion will test whether public budgets absorb it.

Reward blunting is now a measured harm, an addiction treatment and a retail product at once. Growing numbers of lean people take low doses for calm and focus, with no trials in that population, often supplied by the same gray market behind the counterfeit harms.

Thinness has been commoditised and status has moved to muscle, premium agents and monthly dosing. If muscle-sparing combinations and MariTide stay expensive while generic semaglutide stays cheap, the body-as-income signal hardens into a two-tier pharmacology.

A class vision warning is attached to a drug a fifth of adults take, along with rising litigation and a 10-year pediatric registry that has barely begun. The safety picture is being written in real time on a population already committed.

prose.headline: Thin Got Cheap. Now Muscle Is What Money Looks Like.
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2028, about one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, and almost a third have tried one. Efficacy didn't drive most of that climb. Price did. Indian and Canadian generics made the American price look indefensible, and personal-import pens began arriving by mail at a fraction of the domestic cost. Then Novo Nordisk did what insulin makers once did: it launched its own unbranded semaglutide at fifty-nine dollars a month. Lilly cut its oral pill to seventy-nine. Brand exclusivity still runs into the early 2030s, but it no longer protects much.

Cheapness changed who pays. Employers were already retreating, and they took the fifty-nine-dollar sticker as permission to stop; fewer than half now cover weight management. The public sector went the other way. Medicare's bridge pilot was extended instead of being allowed to lapse. In December 2027 Congress lifted the decades-old ban on paying for weight-loss drugs under Part D, effective next year, after cheap semaglutide cut the budget score by more than half. Most Medicaid programs cover the unbranded pen. A federal grant makes it free at community health centres for uninsured adults under twice the poverty line, provided they sit through a nutrition visit. For most new starters, the government is now the payer.

The people left out sit between the lines. One is the home health aide whose employer dropped coverage. Another is the contractor earning just over the threshold. A third is the Medicaid enrollee who misses a work-requirement report and loses three months of coverage. For them the question is no longer whether the drug is affordable but whether this month is. That gap is where the gray market lives. In 2027 the CDC traced hundreds of emergency visits and two deaths to counterfeit pens, some filled with insulin. Customs seizures have multiplied, yet personal importation is still tolerated, a contradiction no one in Washington has resolved. The gray market's most reliable customers are people with no medical case for a prescription at all.

Those customers are the new part of the story. Telehealth brands now sell low-dose plans to lean people for calm, focus and freedom from craving, whether the craving is for snacks, wine, a phone or a cart. In late 2027 addiction-medicine guidelines endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder. The quieting that clinicians had logged as a side effect, and that a 2028 cohort finally measured, became a mechanism in one setting and a product in another. The FTC has warned three companies about their claims, and the category kept growing.

The safety picture is firmer and a little darker. Since February 2027 every GLP-1 drug carries a class warning for sudden optic-nerve vision loss. The absolute risk is small, but at this scale it means thousands of extra cases a year, and the lawsuits followed. Retatrutide arrived in spring 2028 with nearly thirty percent weight loss and a nerve-sensation warning. Amgen's monthly injection was approved in October and is only now reaching pharmacies, priced for the top tier.

The body has re-sorted itself. Anyone can be thin now, so thin means little. What fifty-nine dollars can't buy is muscle: the coach, the protein, the newer drugs that spare lean mass, and the continuity of never having to stop. A large body increasingly reads as uninsured, rural or deliberate. Snack volumes and spirits keep sliding, strength studios keep expanding, and restaurants serve half portions at full price. Some populists say the free shots are sedating the poor. No one has shown it, and the claim travels anyway. From the outside, nothing looks broken.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marisol Ochoa sets two alarms. One is for work. The other is for the first Thursday of the month, when the pharmacy app releases the fifty-nine-dollar pens and they're gone by noon. This month she got them. Last month she didn't, and the pen she used instead came in a padded envelope, its carton printed in a script she couldn't read, and its dial clicked too easily.

At seven she is at Mr. Haskell's. He is eighty-one and on the Medicare one, and he has lost thirty pounds, much of it, she suspects, from his thighs. She spots him from bed to walker. He says he doesn't miss pie. He doesn't miss much, he adds, and she can't tell if that's a complaint.

Lunch is half a turkey wrap in the car. The other half goes back in the foil.

Yesenia, sixteen, texts a photo of a girl from school: shoulders, arms, the defined kind. No caption. Marisol knows what it means. That girl's mother has the good insurance and the gym with coaches. Yesenia wants to know about the new monthly shot. Marisol types back: it's twelve hundred dollars.

At home, Dario is on what his app calls a Quiet plan. It's a low dose he started for focus, though he was never heavy. He doesn't open a beer after work anymore, or argue about the Dodgers. He's easy to be around. She misses arguing.

Before bed she reads the leaflet, the boxed paragraph about sudden vision loss. Left eye closed, then right. The kitchen clock is sharp in both. She injects, caps the pen, and writes the date on the fridge calendar, where she writes everything that might run out.

rationale.badness: This is a recognisably harder society with new losers rather than a catastrophe. Most people gain access: use is 21%, obesity falls to ~33%, and $0 provision reaches the bottom third. The harms are real but moderate: a NAION class label with thousands of excess cases, anhedonia in ~9% of users vs ~5% of controls, counterfeit insulin pens (312 ER visits, 2 deaths), and Medicaid work-requirement churn that induces cycling (1 in 7 with a 60+ day gap). Inequality is rebuilt around muscle and premium agents ('two-tier pharmacology'), and autonomy is bent by a marketed 'calm' layer and by state-induced cycling. The reward-blunting market and children's food environments are structural and under-measured, but the candidate itself says the harm is nameable and measured, so epistemic badness is not extreme. I score it a 5, a harder society and not one most readers would refuse.
rationale.plausibility: The drivers are mostly honoured with visible mechanisms. The NAION label (Feb 2027), counterfeit surge, $59 unbranded Novo pen, AUD guidelines, the subsidy via HRSA, and MariTide approved in Oct 2028 are all present. The chain from the generic collapse to employers dropping coverage to CBO cutting its score is coherent. But several magnitudes strain a two-year window. Adult use roughly doubles to 21.3% (+10.3pp matches the driver), yet ever-use jumps from 15% to 32%. 65+ use goes from 9% to 20% and the 50–64 band from 22% to 32%, which is aggressive. Obesity prevalence falls 3.4pp in two years, and the bottom third rises from ~6% to 18%. Novo launching its own $59 unbranded semaglutide is a plausible insulin-style move, but the cheap price is not well reconciled with Medicare still paying ~$245 for brands. The stipulated driver of an implant-style next-gen is met only by a monthly injection, and the candidate admits 'No implant has reached filing'. Persistence rising to 46% and 4 in 10 children in a user household are generous. Retatrutide approval in Apr 2028 is faster than the BLA timeline allows. A 'significant' gray market alongside $59 legal pens is somewhat in tension. I'd say it needs several generous assumptions.
rationale.generativity: The vignette is rich in concrete texture. Marisol has two alarms, one tied to the pharmacy app's first-Thursday $59 pen drop, and a counterfeit pen with a carton in an unreadable script whose dial 'clicked too easily'. Mr. Haskell, 81, lost weight from his thighs and says he doesn't miss pie. Yesenia, 16, sends the shoulders photo and asks about the $1,200 monthly shot. Dario is on a 'Quiet plan', and the fridge calendar tracks 'everything that might run out'. Class, age, lean-mass loss, the gray market, and the feature-versus-side-effect tension are all shown in scene, not explained. The world fields also imply many more scenes: dating filters, appetite mismatch, the 'sedating the poor' politics, and the Medicaid work-requirement churn.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Medicaid coverage and $0 provision at community health centres pulled the bottom third up from an estimated ~6% to ~18%.
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism/magnitude: free provision at health centres only began Jan 2028, so a threefold jump in bottom-third use within the year is aggressive. The nearby note also says unbranded $59 semaglutide only arrived Aug 2027, which leaves little time to scale.

least_plausible_claims.quote: 65+ use roughly doubled under the extended Medicare bridge.
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude: the bridge only ran from Jul 2026, covers a limited eligible subset (~10% of enrollees) and has copays; the baseline was 9%, so the age band reaching 20% needs a huge uptake. The 20% figure also exceeds the 50-64 share the 2026 baseline implied for comparable groups.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Roughly 3–4% of all adults, mostly affluent, take low 'metabolic health', longevity or 'calm' doses, often outside insurance and partly through the gray market.
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude/mechanism: this adds a very large non-obese cash-pay population (roughly 8-10M people) within about a year of the Nov 2027 guideline and telehealth rollouts, and the 'mostly affluent' claim sits awkwardly with $59 cash pricing and a gray market that supposedly serves the ineligible.

rationale.badness: Aggregate health is arguably improved (obesity 36.4%→33%, near-universal access), offset by a class-vision warning for a fifth of adults, counterfeit harms, state-induced cycling from Medicaid work requirements, and anhedonia in ~9% of users. The world is a recognisably harder society with new losers (the coverage-gap cyclers, older adults losing muscle, lean users on unstudied 'calm' plans), and cohesion strain shows in 'appetite mismatch' and shrinking shared meals. It lands around 5.5 rather than higher because access is broadly widened and the harms are measured and discussable.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: Every driver is visibly present and tied to dated events: NAION label Feb 2027, a $59 unbranded pen (a near-generic), a Medicare extension and HRSA subsidy, AUD plus longevity, monthly MariTide, counterfeits, class stratification and a marketed-feature personality layer. The 'generic_collapse' price path is realised through an authorised generic rather than true generics, which is a minor stretch. mechanism: Most chains are shown, such as the $59 pen driving employers to drop coverage, a lower CBO score enabling the Part D lift, and work requirements causing churn. Several shifts are only asserted, notably the bottom-third rise and the 65+ doubling (claims 1 and 2), and the 3–4% 'wellness' population (claim 3) is thinly tied to the price and gray-market story. magnitude: 21.3% on-drug (+10.3pp) is stipulated, but the layering of retatrutide approval in Apr 2028 (BLA planned Q1 2027), MariTide approval Oct 2028, CagriSema approval, a Part D statute and a 10-year registry all compress the timelines. Subgroup jumps (6→18% bottom third, 65+ doubling, 3–4% of adults on wellness doses) are aggressive, and 32% ever-used while 21% are current implies a figure that is roughly consistent with the note's '1 in 9'.
rationale.generativity: The prose supplies a vivid, grounded protagonist (Marisol: a home health aide with the pen drop on the first Thursday, Mr. Haskell, Yesenia, Dario on a Quiet plan) and many implied scenes. Details like the fridge calendar, the padded-envelope counterfeit pen and 'She misses arguing' give daily life texture. The world JSON also supplies genres and subcultures (dating filters, 'never-on' as identity, sales entertaining) that could each become a film.
